texts: Aelmere is a village on the northern coast.
Aelmere sits at the head of a horseshoe inlet.
Grey cliffs surround the inlet.
Aelmere holds many stone houses.
The houses have slate roofs.
Cauldron Hall stands in Aelmere.
The Watch stands in Aelmere.
The Cliff Path runs along the outer edge of the village.
The Cliff Path runs from the harbor wall to the cliff-spires.
The cliff-spires stand east of the village.
The stones that pave the Cliff Path are flat and sea-worn.
Each Keeper walks the Cliff Path every night.
The Cliff Path holds one hundred and twelve lanterns.
The middle stretch of the Cliff Path is unshielded.
The harbor wall holds twenty-four lanterns.
The fishing boats use the harbor lanterns as beacons at night.
The harbor lanterns are short and squat.
Whenever wind reflects off harbor water at a harbor lantern, that lantern burns its mire-essence quickly.
Harbor-lantern Keepers live near the harbor.
The Sunken Cove lies west of the village.
The Cove Stair leads down to the Sunken Cove.
The Cove Stair is a narrow descending path.
A stone landing stands at the foot of the Cove Stair.
The landing extends into shallow water.
The bones of the old graveyard lie under the water in the Sunken Cove.
When the tide is low, the grave markers are visible below the surface.
The Sunken Cove is cold in every season.
The Stilllight Lantern stands at the top of the Cove Stair.
The Sunken Cove holds a single lantern.
The Stilllight Lantern stands at the Sunken Cove.
The Stilllight Lantern is a large lantern.
The iron bands reinforce the Stilllight Lantern.
The Stilllight Lantern burns through a full night on one filling.
The Stilllight Keeper walks down the Cove Stair at midnight.
The Stilllight Keeper checks the flame at midnight.
The Stilllight Station is the lantern-station at the Sunken Cove.
The Stilllight Station is a demanding station.
Every Keeper fears the Stilllight Station.
The Salt-bloom Tide-pools lie north of the village.
A goat-path along the cliff top leads to the Salt-bloom Tide-pools.
The Salt-bloom Tide-pools are small pools in a stone shelf above the tide-line.
There are seven pools.
Two pools at the south end never bloom.
Whenever a spring tide comes, the tide-pools fill and overflow.
Keepers visit the tide-pools at harvest time.
The Council surveys the tide-pools.
Cauldron Hall is a long low building near the harbor.
Cauldron Hall has thick walls of dark stone.
Cauldron Hall has a tall slate chimney.
Cauldron Hall holds three copper cauldrons.
Each cauldron sits on a stone hearth.
The Council appoints a Keeper as Cauldron Hall Warden each season.
Hesper is the current Cauldron Hall Warden.
Hesper is a careful and silent man.
The Watch is a small square stone hall in the center of the village.
The Watch holds the Council's ledger-room.
The Watch holds the village's feather store.
The feather store is a sealed bin in the floor of the ledger-room.
An iron lid closes the feather bin.
The Council holds keys to the feather bin.
The feather-collectors hold keys to the feather bin.
The Council sits at a long oak table in the Watch.
The Hollows lie inland from the village.
The Hollows are a long stretch of low scrub forest.
Fog usually covers the Hollows.
The Hollows hold thirty-two lanterns.
The lanterns at the Hollows stand along the forest paths.
The lanterns at the Hollows burn dimly.
Keepers keep the lanterns at the Hollows dim.
Whenever a nightmoth flees the Cliff Path, the nightmoth goes to a dim lantern in the Hollows.
A small crew of Keepers tends the Hollows.
The Hollows produce a thin thread harvest.
The Northcove is a small cove.
The Northcove lies north of the village.
Two cliff-spires curve outward around the Northcove.
The cliff-spires shield the Northcove against the north wind.
Thirty lanterns stand in the Northcove.
The Northcove lanterns stand along a curving inner shore.
Northcove lanterns burn through winter.
Northcove lanterns need no salt-bloom.
Northcove lanterns never go out in winter.
The Northcove is a reliable production-row.
The cliff-spires rise above the eastern cliff.
There are nine cliff-spires.
Each cliff-spire is a smooth stone column.
Sea wind weathered the cliff-spires over centuries.
The sky-cats roost on the tops of the cliff-spires.
The cliff-spires are visible from the village.
When sky-cats sit on the cliff-spires in the morning, the day stays calm.
The Cold Sea stretches north of the cliffs.
The Cold Sea is grey-green in summer.
The Cold Sea is slate-grey in winter.
The fishing boats stay near the inlet.
The cold-threshold wind comes off the Cold Sea.
The village square sits between the harbor and the Watch.
A market runs in the village square every week.
Boats from down the coast bring grain, salt, cloth, and ironmongery to the market.
The villagers use the market salt for cooking.
Imported salt does not yield mire-essence.
Every distillation requires sea-water from the Salt-bloom Tide-pools.
The Cauldron Hall cellars lie in the bedrock below the building.
The cellars hold a large reserve of mire-essence.
The cellars are cool and dark.
When a Keeper stores a clay vessel, the Keeper dates that vessel.
The Warden uses old vessels before new vessels.
The Watch ledgers go back many years.
The ledgers record Council decisions, mire-essence reserve levels, feather store levels, apprentice records, and notable events.
Older ledgers were stored in the old Council hall.
The old Council hall collapsed.
The village lost older ledgers.
Forty-three Keepers are active in the present generation.
Pell is a young Keeper.
Pell is a second-year Keeper.
Old Vesh is an old Keeper.
Old Vesh has retired from station-tending.
Old Vesh attends Council.
Old Vesh teaches apprentices.
Meren Tallowhand is the chief Keeper.
Meren Tallowhand tends a Cliff Path station.
Meren Tallowhand is married to Joren Salt.
Joren Salt is a fisherman.
Old Vesh is the village's historian.
Old Vesh retired from active duty eleven years ago.
Old Vesh retired because his hands grew unsteady.
Old Vesh remembers two bad winters.
Old Vesh teaches apprentices the older rituals.
Brindle Coombe sits on the Council.
Brindle Coombe tends a Northcove station.
Brindle Coombe is methodical and even-tempered.
Brindle Coombe delivers the Council's disagreeable announcements.
Sailsworn is a Council member.
Sailsworn is the Salt-bloom Warden for the current year.
The Salt-bloom Warden leads the new-moon harvest expeditions to the tide-pools.
Sailsworn is a reliable cliff-climber.
Hesper is the Cauldron Hall Warden.
Hesper is a Keeper.
Hesper became Warden two years ago.
Hesper does not sit on the Council.
Whenever the moon is full, Hesper reports essence production to the Council.
Coraline Ash is a new apprentice.
Coraline Ash arrived in late summer from down the coast.
Coraline Ash's family farms down the coast.
Coraline Ash is not from a Keeper family.
The Council voted to accept Coraline Ash.
Old Vesh supported Coraline Ash's acceptance.
Pell is Coraline Ash's senior peer.
Pell tends a Cliff Path station near the Hollows junction.
Pell is patient.
Tessa Brae is the village's chief Feather-Collector.
Tessa Brae walks the base of the cliff each morning during the molting season.
Two assistants walk with Tessa Brae.
Tessa Brae became Feather-Collector nine years ago.
Tessa Brae is meticulous about the feather store.
Bevin Coombe is Brindle Coombe's brother.
Bevin Coombe is a Keeper.
Bevin Coombe tends the Stilllight Lantern.
The Stilllight Station is a hard station.
Bevin Coombe sleeps during the day.
Bevin Coombe walks down the Cove Stair every evening at sunset.
Marra Tallowhand is Meren Tallowhand's cousin.
Marra Tallowhand tends a harbor wall station.
Marra Tallowhand keeps a detailed log every night.
Council members often consult Marra Tallowhand's logs.
Each Keeper tends a station alone.
When a Keeper trains an apprentice, the Keeper and the apprentice tend the station together.
When a week is a high-wraith week, two Keepers tend the Stilllight Lantern together.
Night shifts begin at sundown.
Each Keeper checks the lantern at midnight.
Each Keeper checks the lantern at the third watch.
The shift ends at dawn.
Each Keeper carries a leather case.
The case holds a wick-trimmer, a clay flask of mire-essence, a striker, a jar of ground feathers, and a pouch of salt-bloom.
Keepers wear long oilcloth coats.
The coats protect against sea-spray.
Mire-essence stains every Keeper's coat.
Every first-year apprentice wears an unstained coat.
A few Keepers each keep a notebook that lists moth-counts and weather notes.
Whenever an heir inherits a Keeper's lantern-station, that heir inherits that Keeper's notebook.
Two Keepers have left the village.
The two Keepers married outside Aelmere.
Whenever a Keeper leaves a station, the Council assigns an apprentice to that station.
Whenever an apprentice completes thirty solo nights, the Council assigns that apprentice to a station.
There are three apprentices.
Coraline Ash is a first-year apprentice.
Jeb is a second-year apprentice.
Mira is a third-year apprentice.
The Council expects to invest Mira at the next solstice.
Keepers rarely take apprentices from outside Keeper families.
The Council may accept an outside apprentice.
Two earlier outside apprentices became senior Keepers.
Every Keeper considers that lantern-tending is sacred.
Lantern-tending is not religious.
There are no formal prayers.
Meren Tallowhand counts moths aloud while Meren Tallowhand trims the wick.
Bevin Coombe touches the iron bands of the Stilllight Lantern each evening.
The villagers say that the lanterns must burn.
Whenever a birth takes place, a Keeper repeats the phrase.
Whenever a funeral takes place, a Keeper repeats the phrase.
Whenever the Council closes a session, a Keeper repeats the phrase.
The phrase appears in the earliest surviving Watch ledgers.
When a Keeper fails a station, the Council judges that Keeper.
The Council may strip a Keeper of a station.
The Council may assign penance duties.
The Council may bar a Keeper from tending.
The Council has barred two Keepers permanently.
The two barred Keepers often neglected the Stilllight Station.
The village pays each Keeper in food and shelter.
The village pools its fishing harvest, grain trade, and garden produce.
Each Keeper draws a share from the pool.
The villagers use coin for trade with outside merchants.
The Council has seven elders.
The Council appoints new members by consensus.
Council members serve permanently.
A Council member may retire.
The current Council includes Meren Tallowhand, Old Vesh, Brindle Coombe, Sailsworn, Aelis Brae, Norren, and Wynne Coombe.
Wynne Coombe is Brindle Coombe's cousin.
Whenever the moon is full, the Council meets.
The Council meets at sundown in the Watch.
The Council sits at a long oak table.
The oak table is old.
Meren Tallowhand is the Council speaker.
The speaker calls each item of business.
The speaker decides the voting order.
The Council decides by consensus.
When consensus fails, the Council votes by a show of hands.
Every vote is decided by a simple majority.
The speaker breaks a tied vote.
Ties are rare.
Whenever the moon is full, the Council redistributes mire-essence reserves.
Each lantern-station reports its monthly production to the Council.
The Cauldron Hall Warden reports the essence reserve to the Council.
The Council allocates mire-essence to the stations for the coming month.
The Northcove contributes mire-essence to the central pool.
The Stilllight Station draws mire-essence from the central pool.
The exposed Cliff Path stations draw mire-essence from the central pool.
The Council records each redistribution in the ledgers.
The Council decides feather rations.
The Council hears apprentice progress reports.
The Council hears salt-bloom harvest reports.
Whenever a Keeper retires, the Council staffs that Keeper's station again.
Whenever a Keeper dies, the Council staffs that Keeper's station again.
Letters from neighbouring villages are read aloud by the Council.
Two Council members may call an emergency meeting.
Emergency meetings are rare.
The Council has called four emergency meetings.
Three emergency meetings concerned wraith incidents.
One emergency meeting concerned a storm-loss of Cliff Path lanterns.
The Council does not rule on private matters.
Village custom settles marriages and fishing disputes.
The Council decides all Keeper matters.
The Council assigns stations.
The Council decides apprentice investitures.
The Council may discipline Keepers.
The Council may order a Keeper to burn wintergloss.
The Council rarely orders Keepers to burn wintergloss.
A bad winter came one hundred and twelve years ago.
One hundred and twelve years ago, two wraiths emerged in a bad winter.
The salt-bloom harvest failed one hundred and twelve years ago.
The spring tide came at the wrong moon phase one hundred and twelve years ago.
The Council rationed mire-essence after the bad winter of one hundred and twelve years ago.
A very bad winter came sixty-three years ago.
Four wraiths emerged from the Sunken Cove sixty-three years ago.
Old Vesh was a boy sixty-three years ago.
Old Vesh's father was a Keeper sixty-three years ago.
Sixty-three years ago, Old Vesh's father walked the Cove Stair every evening with three Keepers.
The Council created the modern feather-ration system sixty-three years ago.
A bad winter came twenty-six years ago.
Twenty-six years ago, a lone wraith emerged.
Twenty-six years ago, ground feathers around the Stilllight Lantern warded the wraith back.
The Council doubled the feather ration of the Stilllight Station twenty-six years ago.
The ledgers record three near-miss winters.
No wraith emerged in the near-miss winters.
Apprentices study the near-miss winters.
Villages on this coast do not keep lanterns.
Aelmere keeps lanterns.
Faltern lies south of Aelmere.
Keepers from Aelmere exchange letters with the lantern-keepers of Faltern.
The Council recognizes three calendar markers.
The autumn equinox starts moth-season.
The first hard frost starts salt-bloom season.
The spring equinox closes salt-bloom season.
The Council keeps some ledger records secret.
The Council has never opened the secret records.
Keepers sleep during the day.
The village rises late.
The market square is quiet before noon.
The villagers eat a long midday meal.
Each Keeper eats a small meal at sundown before the shift.
Each Keeper carries the leather case to the station at sundown.
Each apprentice walks to the station with a senior Keeper.
The first lighting of a new lantern is a small ritual.
Each Council member touches the vessel of mire-essence before the first lighting.
Replacement lanterns do not need a touch from the Council.
At sundown a Keeper cleans the lantern glass with a soft cloth.
The Keeper trims the wick.
The Keeper fills the reservoir from the day's flask.
When a station needs warding, the Keeper scatters ground feathers around the lantern.
In winter the Keeper sprinkles salt-bloom into the reservoir.
The Keeper lights the wick.
At midnight the Keeper checks the flame.
At midnight the Keeper refills the reservoir to the half-mark.
At the third watch the Keeper trims the wick carefully.
Wicks carbonize over a long burn.
At dawn the Keeper extinguishes the flame with a brass snuffer.
The Keeper walks home after dawn-out.
Tessa Brae walks every part of the base of the cliff each morning during the molting season.
The collectors pick up molted feathers.
The collectors drop the feathers into leather sacks.
The collectors record the collection in a Watch ledger each morning.
The collectors add the feathers to the feather bin.
The salt-bloom new-moon harvest is a large collective ritual.
On the night of the new moon in salt-bloom season, a harvest party walks to the Salt-bloom Tide-pools.
The harvest party wears waxed coats.
The harvest party carries copper buckets.
The harvest lasts until dawn.
The harvest party pours the salt-bloom into the Cauldron Hall salt-bloom store.
Distillation requires sea-water.
In distillation, salt is not a substitute for sea-water.
The Cauldron Hall sea-water store draws from the Salt-bloom Tide-pools.
The sea-water store draws from the deep ebb at the mouth of the harbor.
Three stone cisterns at the back of Cauldron Hall hold the sea-water.
The village holds three festivals each year.
The village holds a feast at Mid-summer during peak moth-season.
Frost-eve is the night before the first hard frost.
The village stockpiles salt-bloom at Frost-eve.
Lantern-night falls at midwinter.
Lantern-night is an important festival.
On Lantern-night every Keeper tends a station.
On Lantern-night every villager walks the Cliff Path at midnight.
The Council speaker lights the Stilllight Lantern at sundown on Lantern-night.
The villagers tell stories around fires in the harbor square on Lantern-night.
Children learn the names of the lantern-stations by heart.
Children chant the station names in games.
Keepers often marry into fisher families.
Whenever a Keeper marries a member of a fisher family, that Keeper keeps the station.
The children of any Keeper may apprentice.
Keeper children may decline apprenticeship.
Some Keeper children do not apprentice.
Those children often fish, farm in the Hollows, or trade down the coast.
The village burns its dead.
There are no graves in Aelmere.
A storm-surge washed the old graveyard into the Sunken Cove six generations ago.
The village cremates the dead at a pyre-shelf on the southern cliff.
The villagers scatter the ashes at sea on the next ebb tide.
Non-Keeper villagers avoid the Sunken Cove.
The villagers consider the Cove Stair unlucky.
The Cove Stair is not forbidden.
Parents scold children who play near the Cove Stair.
A sand-glass in the Watch is the village's clock.
The sand-glass measures one watch.
A watch is a period of the night.
Keepers carry a notched candle for time-keeping.
The Sunken Cove was the village's graveyard six generations ago.
A storm-surge drove water over the cliff edge six generations ago.
The storm-surge washed the graveyard into the inlet.
The bodies and markers settled at the bottom of the Sunken Cove.
The villagers consider the storm-surge the original misfortune of Aelmere.
Wraiths are pale half-translucent figures.
Wraiths rise from the water in the Sunken Cove.
Every Keeper believes that the people who died in the storm-surge became wraiths.
Wraiths do not harm people.
Wraiths drain mire-essence from lit lanterns.
Drained lanterns burn dimly.
Whenever a lantern at the Sunken Cove dies before dawn, a wraith rises from the cove's water.
Keepers know the wraith rule.
The Council enforces strict standards at the Stilllight Lantern.
Wraiths persist for several weeks before they fade back into the cove.
Persisting wraiths approach lit lanterns each night.
Wraiths drain many lanterns while they persist.
When a Keeper scatters ground feathers around a lantern, the feathers ward the lantern against wraiths.
Each feather warding lasts about a month.
Feather warding is the village's primary wraith-defense.
A wraith cannot enter the Watch.
The feather store inside the Watch keeps wraiths out.
A wraith cannot enter Cauldron Hall.
The smell of boiling mire-essence repels wraiths.
No wraith has ever entered a village house.
Twenty-six years ago the Council deliberately let the Stilllight Lantern dim for one night.
The Council wanted to draw the wraith to one place.
Keepers warded the wraith back with ground feathers.
The plan worked.
Every Keeper considers that the plan was dangerous.
No wraith has emerged in the past twenty-six years.
The senior Keepers worry that complacency has crept into the village.
A few Keepers believe that a wraith remembers the Keeper who let that wraith rise.
The Council does not share the superstition.
The villagers tell wraith stories at Lantern-night.
A favorite story concerns the bad winter of sixty-three years ago.
Four wraiths rose sixty-three years ago.
In that winter three Keepers walked the Cove Stair together every evening.
Sky-cats have always lived on the cliff-spires.
The old Watch ledgers mention sky-cats.
Keepers tolerate sky-cats.
Sky-cats are wild animals.
A sky-cat is a small winged animal.
Every sky-cat has broad feathered wings.
Short feather-like fur covers a sky-cat's body.
Sky-cat feathers are mottled grey and white.
Sky-cats fly silently.
Keepers rarely witness a sky-cat hunt.
Sky-cats eat nightmoths.
Sky-cats hunt alone.
Sky-cats roost together.
A dozen sky-cats roost on the cliff-spires.
The keepers cannot count the sky-cats exactly.
The cliff-spires are very high.
Whenever a crowd of nightmoths gathers at a lantern-row, sky-cats descend to hunt.
When a handful of nightmoths gathers at a lantern-row, sky-cats stay on the cliff-spires.
Keepers use the crowd rule.
One sky-cat eats many nightmoths in one night.
After a sky-cat hunts at a lantern-row, the thread harvest at that lantern-row falls.
The nightmoth crowd recovers slowly.
Whenever a sky-cat hunts on the Cliff Path, each nightmoth that survives the hunt flees to the Hollows.
Whenever a sky-cat hunts on the Cliff Path, the lanterns at the Hollows gain nightmoths.
Together, the displaced nightmoths keep the lanterns at the Hollows productive.
Sky-cats molt in late summer.
Sky-cats molt in early autumn.
Whenever a sky-cat molts, feathers fall to the base of the cliff.
Tessa Brae's collectors gather the fallen feathers each morning during the molting season.
Ground feathers of sky-cats ward lanterns against wraiths.
Every Keeper considers that sky-cats are sacred.
Keepers never harm a sky-cat.
Sky-cats sometimes carry a nightmoth to the spires in flight.
Keepers count the visible sky-cats on the cliff-spires each morning.
Keepers track the weight of the feather harvest.
Three sky-cats once hunted nightmoths at the Sunken Cove.
The Council then ordered Bevin Coombe to burn wintergloss at the Stilllight Lantern.
Wraiths that are in the Sunken Cove sometimes harm sky-cats.
When a moth-count at the Stilllight Lantern is low, sky-cats stay on the cliff-spires.
Keepers do not feed sky-cats.
Apprentices never approach the cliff-spires.
The tide rises twice a day.
Spring tides are the large tides of the lunar cycle.
Spring tides occur at new moon or at full moon.
Whenever a spring tide fills the Salt-bloom Tide-pools, salt-bloom blooms in the pools.
Neap tides are the small tides.
Neap tides occur at the quarter moons.
Tide-pools are dry at neap tide.
Salt-bloom needs spring-tide fills.
The new-moon spring tide is the harvest tide.
Whenever a Keeper harvests salt-bloom at the new-moon spring tide, that salt-bloom stays potent for the season.
The Council observes the full-moon spring tide as a calendar marker.
Salt-bloom from the full-moon tide turns to chalky residue.
The keepers cannot explain the moon-phase rule.
The pattern is old and reliable.
Whenever a spring tide ends, a Cauldron Hall apprentice refills the cisterns from the deep ebb.
The apprentice walks the harbor pier to the deep-ebb point.
First-year apprentices usually fill the cisterns.
The cold-threshold wind is a cutting north wind.
Whenever a winter night is clear, the cold-threshold wind comes off the Cold Sea.
The cold-threshold wind chills standing water quickly.
The cold-threshold wind extinguishes unprotected lanterns.
The cold-threshold wind blows between the first hard frost and the spring equinox.
Whenever a Keeper mixes salt-bloom into mire-essence, that mire-essence burns slowly.
Salt-bloomed lanterns survive cold-threshold nights.
Whenever a cold-threshold night comes, unprepared lanterns on the Cliff Path die.
The cold-threshold wind does not reach the Northcove.
Autumn storms come over the Cold Sea.
Early-winter storms come over the Cold Sea.
The autumn equinox begins the storm season.
Autumn storms sometimes destroy Cliff Path lanterns.
The fishing fleet stays near the harbor in winter.
The fleet sails far in summer.
The fleet's safe return depends on the harbor wall lanterns.
A bad winter for lanterns is a bad winter for fishing.
Retreating spring tides sometimes trap small fish in the tide-pools.
Keepers take the trapped fish home on harvest mornings.
The deep ebb is a slow underwater current at the harbor mouth.
The deep ebb runs out of the harbor at low tide.
The water of the deep ebb tastes slightly bitter.
The Cauldron Hall Warden prefers deep-ebb water.
Mire-essence is a thick dark oil.
The smell of mire-essence is faintly metallic.
Mire-essence is dark-green-black.
Mire-essence burns with a pale silver flame.
The pale silver flame of mire-essence is mist-light.
There is no substitute for mire-essence.
Keepers make mire-essence from silken threads and sea-water.
The copper cauldrons produce mire-essence.
Stored mire-essence stays good for years.
The village potter makes the clay vessels.
The clay comes from a seam in the cliffs.
The clay has a green tint.
Silken threads are the deposits that nightmoths leave on lantern rims.
Silken threads are fine, grey, and slightly sticky.
Keepers scrape the threads off the warm stone with a flat blade.
Well-attended lanterns yield a small heap of threads each night in moth-season.
Salt-bloom is a pale crystalline crust.
Whenever a tide-pool stone is submerged, salt-bloom grows on that stone.
Salt-bloom crusts have a faint smell of salt.
Keepers harvest salt-bloom with a wooden scraper.
Iron makes salt-bloom crumble.
The salt-bloom is kept in waxed paper packets in the Cauldron Hall store.
Keepers add salt-bloom to mire-essence in winter.
Whenever a Keeper adds salt-bloom to mire-essence, that mire-essence burns slowly.
A wintergloss is a small flowering plant.
Wintergloss grows in the Hollows.
Wintergloss leaves are dark green and glossy.
Whenever a lantern burns dried wintergloss alongside mire-essence, the wintergloss repels nightmoths from that lantern.
Keepers rarely burn wintergloss.
The village wants nightmoths at its lanterns.
The Council issues wintergloss for the Stilllight Lantern.
Collectors dry the feathers from sky-cats.
Collectors grind the dried feathers in a mortar.
Copper boxes in the Watch hold the ground feathers.
A handful of ground feathers protects a lantern for about a month.
The Council issues feather rations at each full-moon meeting.
The copper cauldrons are old.
A coppersmith family in Faltern forged the cauldrons.
The village cannot replace a lost cauldron.
A brass snuffer is a Keeper's personal tool.
Keepers extinguish the lantern at dawn with a brass snuffer.
Keepers often inherit the snuffer with the station.
A wick-trimmer is a Keeper's personal tool.
A Cliff Path lantern is a heavy stone construction.
Each lantern stands on a stone pedestal.
Every lantern has a glass dome.
A southern glassworks supplies replacement domes.
Every lantern has an iron reservoir for mire-essence.
Each lantern is fixed to its station.
The reservoir of the Stilllight Lantern holds enough mire-essence to burn for one night.
The Council built the Stilllight Lantern sixty-three years ago.
The Council built the Stilllight Lantern because wraiths had risen again and again.
The feather bin is an iron-lidded box in the floor of the ledger-room.
The feather bin holds a large reserve of feathers.
Council members and Tessa Brae hold keys to the feather bin.
The Cauldron Hall salt-bloom store is a wooden cabinet.
Each compartment holds one new-moon harvest.
Hesper dates and labels each harvest.
Keepers use old salt-bloom before new salt-bloom within a season.
Threads arrive at Cauldron Hall each morning.
Each Keeper leaves the night's threads in a wicker basket at the Hall door.
Hesper weighs the threads by mid-morning.
Hesper portions the threads into the three cauldrons.
Hesper draws sea-water from the cisterns.
Hesper pours sea-water over the threads until the threads are submerged.
A banked central hearth lights the cauldron fires.
The central hearth never goes out.
The cauldrons come to a slow boil.
Hesper keeps the cauldrons at a steady simmer.
Whenever a distillation runs in a cauldron and that cauldron boils hard, that distillation fails.
Whenever a cauldron boils hard, that cauldron yields a thin slick of poor essence.
The threads dissolve slowly through the afternoon.
By late afternoon a dark slick forms at the bottom of each cauldron.
The slick is the precursor of mire-essence.
Hesper skims each cauldron at sundown.
Hesper lifts the slick into prewarmed clay vessels with a broad ladle.
Each cauldron yields a vessel that is partly full of mire-essence.
Good threads yield a full vessel.
Poor threads yield a thin slick.
Hesper dates and labels each vessel.
Hesper carries the vessels to the cellars.
The cellar shelves are arranged by year and month.
The old vessels stand at the front of the shelves.
Hesper pours the boiled sea-water into the harbor at the end of the day.
Boiled sea-water does not serve for a second distillation.
Apprentices scrub the cauldrons with sand.
Typical days fill several vessels with mire-essence.
Heavy-thread days fill four vessels with mire-essence.
Thin days fill one vessel with mire-essence.
In deep winter the thread harvest is thin.
Whenever a wraith drains a lantern, the thread harvest at that lantern falls.
When the thread basket is empty, the cauldrons sit idle.
Distillation runs heavily from early autumn to Lantern-night.
The distillation yield thins throughout deep winter.
Distillation recovers from the spring equinox to the summer solstice.
Distillation runs steadily through summer.
Cauldron Hall keeps distillation records.
The records track thread weight, sea-water source, boil time, and vessel yield.
Hesper consults the records for seasonal planning.
One apprentice serves at Cauldron Hall each season.
Jeb served at Cauldron Hall in the autumn of Year 1.
Coraline Ash served at Cauldron Hall briefly in the winter of Year 1.
Moth-counts are thin in deep winter.
Moth-counts recover through spring.
Moth-counts are strong through summer.
The moth-count peaks in early autumn.
The moth-count declines throughout late autumn.
Cold-threshold nights come in stretches of several nights.
Mild periods separate the cold stretches.
Keepers forecast cold-threshold stretches from the spire weathercocks.
Keepers forecast cold-threshold stretches from the hearth smoke.
Sky-cats hunt often in summer.
Sky-cats hunt often in early autumn.
Sky-cats hunt rarely in deep winter.
Sky-cats resume hunting in spring.
When nightmoths are scarce, sky-cats sometimes hunt insects.
Marra Tallowhand's logs record that sky-cats hunt insects.
Nightmoths remain the sky-cats' main food.

rule: X — The Hollows through the year
texts: Whenever a sky-cat hunts on the Cliff Path, the lanterns at the Hollows produce many threads.
In deep winter the lanterns at the Hollows produce a small thread harvest.
In spring the lanterns at the Hollows produce a steady thread harvest.
In summer the lanterns at the Hollows produce a steady thread harvest.
Nine Keepers tend the Hollows.
Keepers at the Hollows often tend lanterns in pairs.
The fog makes the inland paths confusing.
Keepers at the Hollows meet each week at a shed at the forest edge.
Sailsworn inspects the Salt-bloom Tide-pools once each season.
The inspection checks the pools for erosion.
The inspection confirms that the bloom is growing.
Whenever a new year begins, the Council begins a new ledger.
The Council speaker dates the first page of each new ledger.
Meren Tallowhand dated the first page of the current ledger.
Aron Brae is the village potter.
Aron Brae is a cousin of Tessa Brae and Aelis Brae.
Whenever an equinox passes, Aron Brae makes vessels.
Aron Brae fires the vessels in a kiln behind Aron Brae's house.
The clay seam lies at the base of the cliff near the Cove Stair.
A glassworks in Faltern supplies replacement lantern domes.
The village orders new domes in batches.
The glassworks re-fires damaged domes.
The harbor warehouse holds spare domes.
Traders from Faltern and the inland farms come to the market each week.
The market runs from late morning to mid-afternoon in the village square.
The traders sail out before the lanterns are lit.
